Now let me fetch Enduring Word, the Chrysostom homilies, and the biblehub verse pages.I've organised these notes verse by verse. Before you use them, you should know where the gaps are. I ran out of searches before I could find usable comments on vv. 53–57, 59–63 and 66. I found nothing from the NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, the Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), catholic.com or oca.org. And nothing turned up on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this passage. Most of what's here comes from the older commentaries (Barnes, Calvin, Clarke, Coffman, Gill, Ellicott, Matthew Henry, Pulpit Commentary, Wesley) as gathered on biblehub.com and studylight.org. The rest is from Enduring Word, Precept Austin and Chrysostom.

---

## 1. The traditional reading

**v. 51**
- Barnes says the apostles didn't usually carry weapons. On this occasion they had provided "two swords," Luke 22:38, because travellers needed protection from robbers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/26-52.html
- The Light of Israel commentary notes that John 18:10 names the swordsman as Peter and the servant as Malchus, and that Luke says Jesus immediately healed the wounded ear. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/26-52.html
- Matthew Henry says Peter acted without permission. The disciples had asked whether they should strike, But Peter struck before they had an answer. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/26-52.html

**v. 52**
- Ellicott: only Matthew gives Jesus' full words here. The saying is limited in their range by the occasion, because resisting arrest would have meant fighting against God's own purpose. Even so, Ellicott says it is never right to draw the sword "for Christ and His Truth." https://biblehub.com/matthew/26-52.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: the warning is aimed at people who use violence on their own authority. It echoes the ancient law that life is sacred (Genesis 9:5–6). It does *not* predict the Romans destroying the Jews. https://biblehub.com/matthew/26-52.htm
- Barnes thinks the best reading is a warning to Peter, who had rashly attacked the whole armed party on his own. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/26-52.html
- Gill: the saying is about private people who use the sword for revenge, not about magistrates. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/glt/matthew/26-52.html

**v. 53**
- Chuck Smith (Smith's Bible Commentary): Jesus was choosing to submit to His Father. He could have called for angels and didn't need Peter swinging away with his sword. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/26-52.html
- Calvin: the disciples were few and weak, and their attempt to fight a large armed crowd was foolish. Jesus' comparison with the angels makes that folly obvious. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/26-53.html

**v. 54**
- A Bible Hub study note: Jesus refused armed resistance because His death was needed to carry out the Father's plan to save. He willingly gave Himself as the Lamb of God. https://biblehub.com/matthew/26-52.htm
- Matthew Henry: the time had come for Christ to suffer. Peter drawing his sword for Him was like saying Master, spare thyself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/26-52.html

**v. 56**
- Precept Austin: all eleven disciples fled, and this fulfilled prophecy. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary

**v. 58**
- Enduring Word: Peter was determined to prove Jesus wrong about the coming denial. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/
- Matthew Henry: following Christ "afar off" was where Peter's denial began, for to follow him afar off, is by little and little to go back from him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_026.cfm
- Coffman suggests that if Peter had stayed close, like the "other disciple" (probably John), he might not have denied Jesus. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/matthew-26.html
- Precept Austin: the whole failure came from letting too much distance grow between Peter and the Lord. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary

**v. 64**
- Clarke takes "You have said it" to mean *I am the Christ*. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/26-64.html
- Barnes: "Power" here is a name for God, and sitting at a ruler's right hand was the chief place of honor. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/26-64.html
- Gill: Jewish writings often call God "the Power." The Sanhedrin would "see" Christ's exaltation through its effects, such as the Spirit being poured out at Pentecost and the spread of the gospel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/26-64.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: Jesus is here claiming to be divine, applying Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13–14 to Himself. https://biblehub.com/matthew/26-64.htm

**v. 65**
- Ellicott: tearing the robe was almost as much a formal sign of condemnation as the putting on of the black cap by an English judge. https://biblehub.com/matthew/26-65.htm
- Was it against the law (Leviticus 21:10)? Commentators disagree:
  - Clarke says tearing the high priest's garments was flatly against the law. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/26-65.html
  - Barnes and Gill say the ban covered only the priestly vestments, not the clothes Caiaphas had on, and Jewish custom required anyone who heard blasphemy to tear his garments. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/26-65.html
- Calvin: the gesture shows how people who despise God fake zeal for Him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/26-65.html
- Barnes: the "blasphemy" was that Jesus, under oath, claimed what belongs to God alone. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlt/matthew/26-65.html

**vv. 67–68**
- Chrysostom: the mockery shows the leaders' cruelty, and the Gospel writers' honesty in reporting such shameful things shows their love of truth. Isaiah had foretold it. Christians should take pride in Christ's sufferings, not only in His miracles. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/200185.htm

**vv. 69–74**
- Enduring Word: Peter's sin got worse each time. First, he merely lied; then he took an oath to the lie; then he began to curse and swear. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/
- Bible Hub study note on v. 74: by calling Jesus "the man," Peter cuts himself off from any personal tie to Him. https://biblehub.com/study/matthew/26-74.htm
- Chrysostom: the same man who had boldly drawn a sword now couldn't face a lowly servant girl. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/200185.htm
- Rooster crowing once or twice (Matthew vs. Mark 14:72): Pulpit Commentary, Norman Geisler (quoted by Precept Austin) and Chrysostom all say the accounts agree. Mark simply gives more detail.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/matthew/26.htm
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary
  - https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/200185.htm

**v. 75**
- Matthew Henry: after weeping, Peter never denied Christ again but confessed Him openly. True repentance shows itself in practising the opposite virtue. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_026.cfm
- Precept Austin: Peter was forgiven, restored and sent out (John 21:15–19). https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-26-commentary

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

**v. 52 – Does this forbid Christians to use force?** This is the clearest disagreement I found.
- **Reformed (Calvin):** Jesus confirms that the Law forbids private individuals to use the sword. Lawful self-defence would have to be free of anger and revenge, which scarcely ever happens. But Calvin calls "fanatics" those who use this verse to take the sword away from magistrates. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/26-52.html
- **Lutheran (Luther, as quoted in Meyer's commentary):** "Those take the sword who use it without proper authority." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/26-52.htm
- **Methodist (Adam Clarke):** Neither Christ nor his religion is to be defended by the secular arm. A private person should not resist even the appearance of public justice. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/26-52.html
- **Restoration Movement (Coffman):** the verse doesn't reject the sword's proper place in society. Jesus told Peter to put it "in its place," not throw it away. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/26-52.html
- **"Contending for the Faith" commentary (on the same StudyLight page):** this commentator reads Jesus as teaching pacifism. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/26-52.html
- **Early church (as reported by a Bible Hub article):** Justin Martyr cites this verse to show Christians no longer fight with the sword. The same article insists Romans 13:4 shows the saying is about personal revenge, not the state. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_live_by_sword_die_by_sword.htm

**v. 64 – When will they "see" this?**
- **Reformed (Geneva Bible notes):** the word "hereafter" separates Christ's first coming from His second. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/26-64.htm
- **Methodist (Wesley):** links the verse to Daniel 7:13–14 and remarks that Jesus "looked very unlike that person now." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/26-64.html
- **Benson (Methodist):** the proofs of Christ's power at God's right hand were Pentecost, the spread of the gospel and the destruction of Jerusalem. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/26-64.html
- **Clarke:** "hereafter" means within a few years, when Christ would judge the nation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/26-64.html
- **Other options (from the Bible Hub commentary page):** Poole sets out three readings: soon (resurrection, ascension, Pentecost), the Day of Judgment, or both. Meyer cites Beza and others for a figurative "coming." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/26-64.htm
- **Futurist reading (a modern Bible Hub summary):** looks ahead to a literal, visible Second Coming. https://biblehub.com/matthew/26-64.htm

**vv. 69–75 – Did Peter lose his faith?**
- **Enduring Word (David Guzik, Calvary Chapel):** Peter's weeping shows backsliding, not apostasy like Judas. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-26/
- On John 18, Guzik adds that it was not the faith of Peter that failed, but his courage. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-18/

## 3. Other views

**Modern scholarship**
- v. 52: Weiss (in Meyer, Expositor's Greek Testament) doubted Jesus said this here, seeing it as a loose reworking of Revelation 13:10. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/26-52.htm
- vv. 69–75: Enduring Word reports that New Testament scholar Robert Gundry argues Matthew presents Peter as a false disciple and apostate. Gundry points to the denial "before all" (v. 70) and the oath (v. 72). Guzik disagrees: Matthew never calls Peter "the denier," the way he calls Judas "the betrayer." https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/thinking-about/was-peter-a-false-disciple-and-apostate/

**Catholic and Orthodox (Church Fathers)**
- v. 52: Calvin attacks some Catholic canon lawyers who taught that Peter was only told to keep his sword sheathed until the right time came. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/26-52.html
- v. 52: Chrysostom says Jesus restored the servant's ear and used the warning to calm Peter's hot temper. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/240183.htm
- v. 65: Pulpit Commentary says the Fathers saw the torn robe as a symbol of the rending and destruction of the Jewish priesthood. https://biblehub.com/matthew/26-65.htm
- Peter's denial: Chrysostom says Christ allowed it to break Peter's self-confidence, and the other disciples learned human weakness from it. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/200182.htm
- v. 75: Chrysostom says Peter went outside to weep so his tears wouldn't give him away. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/200185.htm
